title: Waived Molecular POCT: Influenza, Strep A and the Culture-Backup Question
summary: Learn what makes a molecular test CLIA-waived, which assay was the first waived molecular point-of-care test, why the culture-backup rule for Strep A belongs to the antigen era, how influenza guidelines rank rapid molecular tests, and what can still go wrong in a sealed cartridge.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 7 Hits 7, 8 and 11 and Trap 4. Checked against Deak and Marlowe 2017, Gonzalez and McElvania 2018, Schmitz 2022, Pellegrino 2023, and the IDSA guidelines for Strep A pharyngitis (Shulman 2012) and influenza (Uyeki 2019), both IDSA guidelines read via a page-fetch tool (first part of each page only). Hit 7 names Roche Liat as the first CLIA-waived molecular test; Deak and Marlowe 2017 name the Alere i Influenza A&B (2015), so the lesson teaches the source (register flag rv-first-waived-molecular). Hit 8 and Trap 4 say culture backup of negative molecular tests is no longer needed; the sources say it “may not” be required and that guidelines do not yet address POC NAAT (register flag rv-gas-molecular-backup). An FDA press release on the Alere i waiver could not be retrieved (404). Not taught as fact: “five manufacturers” of POC molecular flu tests, the Liat Group A Strep 97.2% concordance and 6.6% failure figures, cost figures, and the claim that operator error specifically causes false negatives. US-only; Philippine rules are not covered.

objectives: State the FDA criterion for a CLIA-waived test and name the first CLIA-waived molecular point-of-care test.
Explain why the culture-backup rule for negative Strep A tests was written for antigen tests, and what limits molecular Strep A tests still have.
Name the main risks of waived molecular testing outside the laboratory.

scenes.title: Molecular testing leaves the lab
scenes.altText: Schematic: a sealed cartridge with three internal steps (extract → amplify → detect). Cards: “CLIA-waived” = FDA criterion: so simple and accurate that erroneous results are negligible, or no reasonable risk of harm if performed incorrectly; non-laboratorians may perform it following the manufacturer’s instructions. “First CLIA-waived molecular POC test” = Alere i Influenza A&B, 2015 (Deak and Marlowe 2017). “cobas Liat” = real-time PCR, CLIA-waived, influenza A/B with RSV and Strep A assays. “Built-in QC” = some tests include internal electronic and reagent QC and shut down after failed QC.

cues.text: A CLIA-waived test is one the FDA judges so simple and accurate that errors are negligible, or one that poses no reasonable risk of harm if done incorrectly. Non-laboratorians may run it by following the manufacturer’s instructions.
Molecular point-of-care tests put extraction, amplification and detection inside one sealed cartridge, so nurses and physicians can run them in a clinic.

The first CLIA-waived molecular point-of-care test was the Alere i Influenza A and B assay, in 2015. Roche’s cobas Liat, a real-time PCR system, has waived assays for influenza A and B with RSV, and for Strep A.
Some of these tests build in electronic and reagent quality control, and shut down when that control fails.

scenes.title: Strep A: the culture-backup rule
scenes.altText: Left card, IDSA 2012 (antigen era): children and adolescents: back up a negative rapid antigen detection test (RADT) with a throat culture; adults: routine backup culture not necessary; positive RADT: no backup needed (highly specific). Right card, molecular POC: high sensitivity (for example, one assay 98.7% sensitive vs culture in 481 mainly paediatric specimens, run by non-laboratory staff); a review states these tests “may not require reflex to culture”; the 2012 guideline does not address NAAT, and a 2023 guideline comparison found the role of POC NAAT is not discussed in current guidelines. Limits token: test only symptomatic patients (carriers), not a test of cure (detects dead organisms), misses groups C and G unless the assay targets them.

cues.text: The culture-backup rule was written for antigen tests. The 2012 IDSA guideline says a negative rapid antigen test in a child or adolescent should be backed up by throat culture. Adults do not routinely need it, and a positive antigen test needs no backup.

Molecular point-of-care tests are more sensitive than antigen tests. In one multicentre study, run by non-laboratory staff, a waived assay detected about ninety-nine percent of culture-positive throats.

So a review concludes that a negative molecular test may not need reflex culture. But the 2012 guideline predates these tests, and a 2023 comparison found current guidelines do not address them, so follow the assay instructions and local policy.

Sensitivity has a price. Molecular tests find carriers, so test only patients with symptoms. They detect dead organisms, so they are not a test of cure. And group A assays miss groups C and G streptococci unless the assay also targets them.

props.label: Carriers · dead organisms · groups C/G missed

scenes.title: Influenza and the hook answers
scenes.altText: Influenza card (IDSA 2018): outpatients: use rapid molecular assays rather than rapid antigen tests (RIDTs); hospitalised patients: RT-PCR or other molecular assays; pooled rapid molecular sensitivity about 92% (A) and 95% (B), specificity about 99%; a negative may not rule out influenza; false positives possible when positive predictive value is low. Contamination card: amplification makes amplicons that can cross-contaminate; self-contained sealed systems significantly reduce that risk; errors arise when non-laboratory staff do not understand QC and specimen handling. Hook answers: (1) negative molecular Strep A in a child: assay instructions and local policy decide whether to culture; (2) negative rapid molecular flu with strong suspicion: a negative may not rule out influenza; (3) a sealed cartridge lowers contamination risk but quality-control and handling errors can still occur.

cues.text: Influenza follows the same logic. The 2018 IDSA guideline prefers rapid molecular assays over antigen tests in outpatients, and RT-PCR or other molecular assays in hospitalised patients.

Pooled sensitivity of rapid molecular assays was about ninety-two percent for influenza A and ninety-five percent for B, with specificity near ninety-nine. A negative may not rule out flu, and a false positive is possible when positive predictive value is low.

The big worries: amplification makes amplicons that can contaminate the next test and give false positives. Self-contained, sealed systems significantly reduce that risk, but errors can still arise when staff do not understand quality control and specimen handling.
Hook answers: the child’s negative strep test follows the assay instructions and local policy. The adult’s negative flu test may not rule out flu. And yes, a sealed cartridge can still go wrong.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Roche Liat was the first CLIA-waived molecular test” (✓ a 2017 review names Alere i Influenza A&B, 2015, as the first CLIA-waived molecular POC test); “Every negative molecular Strep A must be cultured” (✓ the backup rule was written for antigen tests; molecular tests may not need it: follow the assay and local policy); “A sealed cartridge cannot give a false result” (✓ a sealed design lowers contamination risk, but quality-control and handling errors still occur).

cues.text: Trap one: Roche’s Liat was the first CLIA-waived molecular test. A 2017 review names the Alere i Influenza A and B test, in 2015.
Trap two: every negative molecular strep test must be cultured. The backup rule belonged to antigen tests; a negative molecular test may not need it, so check the assay and local policy.
Trap three: a sealed cartridge cannot give a false result. A sealed design lowers contamination risk, but quality-control and handling errors can still happen.

cues.text: Memory aid: a waived molecular test is a lab in a lunchbox. The whole PCR lab is packed inside, so it is sensitive. But whoever carries it must pick the right patient, the right swab, and keep the box clean.

Where it breaks: performance differs between assays, guidelines have not settled the culture question, and a sensitive test still cannot tell a carrier from an infection or detect organisms it does not target.

scenes.altText: Two tokens: “First waived molecular POC test: Alere i Influenza A&B (2015) · Liat: flu/RSV, Strep A”, “Culture backup = antigen-era rule · molecular: insert + local policy · contamination and operator errors persist”.

explanation.what: Plain language: PCR-type tests now come in sealed cartridges that clinic staff can run in minutes. They are much more sensitive than the old quick antigen tests, but they can still be fooled by carriers, contamination and handling mistakes. Scientific terms: CLIA-waived test, molecular point-of-care (mPOC) test, nucleic acid amplification test (NAAT), rapid antigen detection test (RADT), rapid influenza diagnostic test (RIDT), RT-PCR, isothermal amplification, amplicon contamination, positive predictive value, carriage.
explanation.why: Antigen tests miss many infections, so negatives in children needed culture backup and negative flu antigen tests may need confirmation. Putting amplification at the point of care brings near-laboratory sensitivity to the visit, but the testing is done by people without laboratory training, outside the laboratory’s pre-analytical filters.
explanation.measure: Waived: FDA criterion “so simple and accurate as to render the likelihood of erroneous results negligible” or “no reasonable risk of harm” if performed incorrectly. First waived mPOC: Alere i Influenza A&B, 2015. IDSA 2012: culture a negative RADT in children/adolescents; not routinely in adults; no backup for a positive. Molecular Strep A: one waived assay 98.7% sensitive and 98.5% specific vs culture (481 specimens); “may not require reflex to culture”. IDSA 2018 influenza: rapid molecular over RIDT for outpatients; RT-PCR or other molecular for inpatients; pooled sensitivity about 92% (A) and 95% (B), specificity about 99%.
explanation.differs: Antigen RADT (needs culture backup in children) vs molecular POC (may not); rapid molecular vs laboratory RT-PCR (rapid may be somewhat less sensitive and specific); sealed self-contained systems vs open amplicon handling (contamination risk greatly reduced, not zero).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: name the first waived molecular test, decide whether a negative strep test needs culture (antigen vs molecular), pick the preferred influenza test for an outpatient or inpatient, or name a risk of waived molecular testing.

questions.stem: According to the 2012 IDSA guideline, which negative Strep A result should be backed up by a throat culture?

options.text: A negative rapid antigen test in a 9-year-old with pharyngitis
options.rationale: Correct. In children and adolescents, a negative RADT should be backed up by throat culture because antigen tests miss infections.

options.text: A negative rapid antigen test in a healthy 35-year-old adult
options.rationale: Incorrect. Routine backup culture is not necessary for adults in usual circumstances.

options.text: A positive rapid antigen test in a child
options.rationale: Incorrect. Positive RADTs are highly specific and need no backup culture.

options.text: Any patient with cough, runny nose and mouth ulcers
options.rationale: Incorrect. Features that strongly suggest a viral cause mean Strep A testing is usually not recommended at all.

questions.stem: Which statement about waived molecular point-of-care tests for Strep A is correct?

options.text: They can detect carriers, so they should be used only in patients with symptoms of pharyngitis
options.rationale: Correct. Their high sensitivity detects colonisation, so testing should be limited to symptomatic patients.

options.text: They are a good test of cure after antibiotic treatment
options.rationale: Incorrect. Molecular tests do not distinguish live from dead organisms.

options.text: They always detect groups C and G streptococci
options.rationale: Incorrect. Group A assays do not detect groups C and G; only some assays add those targets.

options.text: They are less sensitive than rapid antigen tests
options.rationale: Incorrect. Molecular tests are more sensitive than antigen tests, which is why culture backup may not be needed.

questions.stem: Under the 2018 IDSA influenza guideline, which test is preferred for an outpatient with suspected influenza?

options.rationale: Correct. Rapid molecular assays are recommended over rapid influenza antigen tests in outpatients to improve detection.
Incorrect. RIDTs are less sensitive; the guideline prefers rapid molecular assays.
Incorrect. Culture is too slow to guide treatment at the visit.

options.text: Serology on a single serum sample
options.rationale: Incorrect. Single-sample serology does not diagnose acute influenza for clinical decisions.
